reviews.quote: The Steam Deck OLED impresses thanks to its vibrant display, lighter design, faster Wi-Fi and improved cooling... this latest iteration demonstrates that Valve can improve on perfection. The Steam Deck OLED has set a new standard for competitors to follow.
This isn't the Steam Deck 2 some are waiting for, it's just a welcome improvement on an already good device.
Though the Xbox Ally and Legion Go (S and 2) lines offer larger batteries than the Steam Deck OLED, in real-world applications, Valve's handheld often comes out on top.

praises: OLED HDR at 90Hz is 'night and day' vs the LCD even at the same 1280x800 — pure blacks make night-time gaming dramatically better
Battery is genuinely 30-50% better than LCD and 20-80% charge in 45 minutes makes couch top-ups painless
SteamOS sleep/resume, quick-access menu and game verification labels make it feel like a console, not a Windows handheld
iFixit 10/10 repairability — Valve sells its own stick modules, SSD, battery and shell parts; standard M.2 2230 SSD
Noticeably cooler and quieter than the LCD under load; larger fan is 'not any louder' per Engadget
complaints: Same 2021-era Zen 2/RDNA2 APU — UE5 and new AAA games need 20-30fps caps and still stutter; no performance gain over 2022 LCD
2025-26 CAD price increases (now C$1,349) hurt value vs faster Xbox Ally X / Legion Go 2 at similar money
Still huge and heavy (640g, 11.7in wide) — 'a Wii U, not a Vita'; uncomfortable for small hands in long sessions
SteamOS cannot run anti-cheat multiplayer titles (Fortnite, CoD: Warzone), pushing some users to dual-boot Windows
microSD slot is slow UHS-I (~90MB/s) so expanded library games load noticeably slower than internal SSD

design_philosophy: Valve's bet that open PC gaming can be packaged as a console: a mid-cycle OLED refresh (die-shrunk APU, better screen/battery/thermals) deliberately keeping the 2022 chassis, controls, and performance target so the whole Steam library stays the platform. This 512GB OLED is the volume sweet spot of the current lineup.
